passage: Kwame had reported the blocked fire exit in his Leeds hall of residence back in October. It was now February, and the door was still chained. He had emailed the housing office twice and got the same auto-reply both times. "They don't care," he told Rania in the kitchen, jabbing at a slice of toast. "It's the same everywhere. What's the point?" Rania, the peer adviser from the students' union, leaned on the counter. "The housing office isn't the only route. There's the union's advice service, and a formal complaints process with a deadline." "You believe that works?" "Sometimes. It took me two tries once." That night Kwame wrote out the dates, attached the photos he'd taken, and sent it to the union adviser. Three weeks later the chain was gone, and Kwame stood in the doorway a moment, a little surprised.

qa.q: Where was the blocked fire exit that Kwame reported?
qa.a: It was in his Leeds hall of residence.

qa.q: How did Kwame feel about systems after the housing office's replies?
qa.a: Cynical and discouraged, as he said they don't care and asked what the point was.

qa.q: What did Kwame do that worked when the first channel failed?
qa.a: He took a different route, sending his dated report and photos to the union's advice service.

qa.q: What is it like for Rania when Kwame says the process is pointless?
qa.a: Rania probably feels a mix of understanding and hope, since Rania admits it once took two tries yet still believes it can work.

grounding: The protagonist reported and nothing happened, feels cynical about systems, then tries another channel with help from people who know the process.

passage:
Exam week, a power cut, and a phone at eight percent. Jasleen sat on the hostel stairs by candlelight and read the reply to her complaint about the locked fire exit on the third floor: "Noted. Will be looked into." It was the same reply she'd got in August. The door was still chained.

She felt a hard, tired bitterness. Nothing works. Every office is the same. Why bother?

Devika from the student rights group found her there. "Still chained?" Jasleen nodded.

"Then we try another door. The fire department does inspections if residents ask. And the university has a safety committee with student members."

"And if they do nothing too?"

"Then we keep going. Some things take three tries."

After her last exam Jasleen wrote to the fire department, with Devika's group signing too. Two weeks later, an officer visited. The chain came off that afternoon.

qa.a: Jasleen's complaint was about the locked fire exit on the third floor.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling when she read the reply?
qa.a: Jasleen felt bitter and tired, cynical that no office would ever act.

qa.q: What did Devika suggest, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Devika suggested other channels, the fire department and the safety committee, and joining others who knew the process, so the problem got real attention.

qa.q: How might Devika see Jasleen's cynicism?
qa.a: Devika seems to understand it but believes change often takes several tries, so she offers another route instead of agreeing that nothing works.

grounding: The story shows a young woman cynical after a report went nowhere, trying another channel with a group that knows the process.

passage:
Gopika had reported the broken drain cover outside the Chennai school gate on the city complaint portal in June. In July, a child fell in up to the knee. In August she reported again and got an automatic message: "Your complaint has been resolved." The drain was still open.

She told everyone at her office tea break: "The whole system is a joke. Nobody is ever going to fix anything. Don't waste your time."

Imran, from accounts, listened. "My residents' association got our streetlights fixed last year. Took them three routes. Want to come to their meeting Saturday?"

She almost said no. She went.

The association knew the ward councillor's office hours, the name of the engineer in charge, and how to escalate a closed complaint. Gopika went with two of them on Monday, with her photos. By Friday a new cover was in place. She still didn't trust the portal. But she trusted people a little more.

qa.q: What did the automatic message say?
qa.a: It said, "Your complaint has been resolved."

qa.q: How did Gopika feel after the second report failed?
qa.a: Gopika felt bitter and disillusioned, sure that nobody would ever fix anything.

qa.q: How did joining the residents' association help?
qa.a: The association knew the councillor's hours, the engineer's name and how to escalate, so another channel worked where the portal failed.

qa.q: How might the child who fell in have been affected if nobody kept trying?
qa.a: The child, and others, would keep facing danger every day at the school gate.

grounding: The story shows a young woman cynical after a report was ignored, trying another channel through a group that knows the process and keeping some faith in change.
